title: Midnight in the jail (Acts 16:25–34)
hook: Paul and Silas sing hymns in chains, and the jailer asks what must I do

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lydia, the seller of purple by the river. Your line was the lord opened her heart. Who did you invite in? Day five hundred fifty.

Still in Philippi, a few days later. A slave girl who tells fortunes earns her owners a lot of money. Paul, worn out by her following them around, casts the spirit out of her, and her owners see their profits walk away. They drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates. A crowd joins in. The two are stripped, beaten with rods, thrown into the inner prison, and their feet are fastened in the stocks. Bruised, bleeding, in the dark. A night like that could be spent in anger, or fear, or silence.
screen: `THE FORTUNE-TELLER'S OWNERS.` → `BEATEN WITH RODS.` → `FEET IN THE STOCKS.`

segments.voice: Here's what they do instead. In the Douay-Rheims: "And at midnight, Paul and Silas praying, praised God." The Greek says they were singing hymns. And then a detail Luke didn't have to include: "they that were in prison, heard them." Picture it. A dark cell, men in chains, and two of the newest arrivals singing. Suddenly there's an earthquake. The foundations shake, every door flies open, and everyone's chains come loose. The jailer wakes up, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, since a jailer who lost his prisoners could expect to answer for it. And Paul cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do thyself no harm, for we all are here." Nobody ran. The jailer calls for a light, rushes in trembling, falls down before them, and asks the question at the center of today: "Masters, what must I do, that I may be saved?" Their answer is short: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your house. That same night, the man who locked their feet in the stocks washes their wounds. Then he and his whole household are baptized. He brings them into his house, sets food before them, and rejoices. Look at the shape of it. Songs in the dark, then an open door no one walks through, then a jailer washing wounds. Years later, writing to this same church from another prison, Paul tells the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord always.
screen: `AT MIDNIGHT, PRAYING, THEY PRAISED GOD.` · `THE PRISONERS WERE LISTENING.` · `DO THYSELF NO HARM, FOR WE ALL ARE HERE.` · `WHAT MUST I DO, THAT I MAY BE SAVED?` · then, large: `THE JAILER WASHES THEIR WOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing in a hard place. Settle, and breathe. Think of the hardest place in your life right now, a worry, a room, a relationship. Now pick a song you know by heart. A hymn, if you have one: Amazing Grace, a Marian hymn, anything from Mass. Or any song that has carried you before. Hum a line of it, or just hear it in your head, right there in the hard place. You don't have to feel cheerful. Paul and Silas had bleeding backs. If you pray, the song can be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Midnight in the jail. Paul and Silas singing in chains, an earthquake, and a jailer who asks what must I do, then washes their wounds. Today's word.
Your line: singing at midnight. Today, when it gets hard, hum one line of a song that carries you. Day five hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours through the day and night, singing psalms and hymns, and the Church counts visiting the imprisoned among the works of mercy.

fork.setup: you're Paul. an earthquake has opened every door and loosed your chains. the jailer is about to kill himself. what do you do?
options: slip out in the dark while you can.
cry out: do thyself no harm, for we all are here.
fork.reveal: Paul stops him. the man who locked them in asks what he must do to be saved, washes their wounds, and is baptized with his household.

original.note: Greek: they were singing hymns. what Paul and Silas did at midnight, the root of our word hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a jailbreak miracle.
what it means: two beaten men sing in the dark, refuse to escape, and the jailer who chained them becomes the one who washes their wounds.
what a scholar hears: the Greek says they were singing hymns, which the Latin and Douay render as praying, they praised God. and a Roman guard who lost prisoners could face their penalty himself.

notes: Confirm the Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 16:25 and the KJV wording of 16:25, 16:28 and 16:30.
Greek hymnoun (imperfect, 'were singing hymns') and the Vulgate 'laudabant Deum': confirm.
Roman guards facing their prisoners' penalty (compare Acts 12:19): confirm phrasing.
Philippians written from prison: traditional and widely held; the place of imprisonment is debated.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: three KJV quotations (16:25, 16:28, 16:30) on the Catholic path replaced with the Douay-Rheims, verified ('they that were in prison, heard them'; 'Do thyself no harm, for we all are here'; 'Masters, what must I do, that I may be saved?'); screens, myth and fork follow. Cut 'most of us would spend that night angry' (telling the listener) and 'the Church has always'; the jailer's penalty softened to 'expect to answer for it'.
